items.title: What makes a good tax
items.rule:
Adam Smith's four canons: a good tax is fair (linked to ability to pay), certain (amount and timing clear, not arbitrary), convenient (easy to pay) and efficient (cheap to collect).

Three principles of tax policy: equity (burden shared fairly), efficiency (low collection cost, e.g. PAYE) and economic effects (how collection affects behaviour).
items.body:
Governments tax to fund spending and service debt, and to steer behaviour (capital allowances encourage investment; duties on tobacco discourage it).

The AICPA extends the list to ten: equity, transparency, certainty, economy in collection, convenience, simplicity, appropriate revenues, minimum tax gap, neutrality, growth. No real system meets all ten.
items.trap: "Progressive" is not one of Smith's canons. Fairness is, and progressivity is only one way to deliver it.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Adam Smith's canons of a good tax?
opts: Fairness, linked to the ability to pay
Certainty of amount and timing
Convenience of payment
Progressive rates as income rises
sol: Smith's four canons are fair, certain, convenient and efficient.
Progressive rates are one design choice for achieving fairness, not a canon in their own right.
items.trap: Picking "fairness" because it sounds political. It is a canon.

alt.q: Which of the following IS one of Adam Smith's canons of a good tax?
opts: Hypothecation of revenue
Efficiency: cheap to collect
Neutrality between industries
Progressive rates as income rises
sol: The canons are fair, certain, convenient and efficient.
Neutrality is an AICPA principle, not one of Smith's four. Hypothecation is ring-fencing, not a canon.
alt.trap: Neutrality appears on the AICPA list of ten, which is easy to confuse with Smith's four.

items.title: Direct v indirect taxes
items.rule:
Direct: charged on the person who bears it, based on income, profits or gains. They pay the authority themselves.

Indirect: charged at one point in the supply chain on spending, and intended to be passed on to the final consumer.
items.body:
TypeExamples
DirectIncome tax, corporate income tax, capital gains tax, inheritance tax, property tax
IndirectVAT / sales tax, excise duties, customs duties
items.trap: Employee income tax collected through PAYE is still direct. The employer only collects it; the employee bears it.

items.title: Corporate v personal taxes
items.rule:
Corporate taxes fall on the entity: corporate income tax on taxable profit, with company gains usually taxed inside it.

Personal taxes fall on individuals: income tax on earnings (salary, bonus, benefits in kind), personal capital gains tax and social security contributions.
items.body:
The same profit can be taxed twice: once in the company, then again when it reaches a shareholder as a dividend. Chapter 2 covers the four systems countries use to deal with that.

The company is still involved in personal tax: it withholds employees' income tax through PAYE and pays employer social security.
items.trap: A tax the company pays over is not necessarily a corporate tax. PAYE is personal tax collected by the company.

items.q: Consider (i) duty on fuel, (ii) employee income tax collected through payroll, (iii) corporate income tax and (iv) general sales tax. Which are direct taxes?
opts: (i) and (ii)
(i) and (iv)
(ii) and (iii)
(ii) and (iv)
sol: Direct = charged on the income or profit of the person who bears it.
Employee income tax (ii) and corporate income tax (iii) are direct.
Fuel duty (i) and sales tax (iv) are on spending and passed on, so they are indirect.
items.trap: Thinking payroll tax is indirect because the employer pays it over. The employee bears it, so it is direct.

alt.q: Consider (i) duty on fuel, (ii) employee income tax collected through payroll, (iii) corporate income tax and (iv) general sales tax. Which are indirect taxes?
sol: Indirect = charged on spending and passed on to the consumer.
Fuel duty (i) and general sales tax (iv) are indirect.
Income tax (ii) and corporate income tax (iii) are direct.
alt.trap: Treating PAYE as indirect because the employer collects it.

items.q: Which TWO of these are direct taxes?
opts: General sales tax
Inheritance tax
Customs duty
A local property tax
sol: Inheritance tax is on capital/wealth passing on death, borne by the estate: direct.
A property tax is charged on the owner by reference to the property's value: direct.
Sales tax and customs duty are on spending or imports and passed on: indirect.

alt.q: Which TWO of these are indirect taxes?
sol: Sales tax and customs duty are charged on spending or imports and passed on: indirect.
Inheritance tax and property tax are charged on the person who bears them: direct.

items.flag: The kit shows single-choice buttons here but accepts both B and D. It is set up as select-two in this app so either answer is not marked wrong.

items.q: Which is an example of an indirect tax?
opts: A company pays tax on its taxable profits
A diner pays a restaurant bill that includes sales tax
An employee's pay has income tax deducted
An investor pays tax on a gain from selling shares
sol: Sales tax is built into the price and borne by the customer: indirect.
Corporate tax, employee income tax and capital gains tax are all direct.

alt.q: Which is an example of a direct tax?
opts: A shopper pays a price that includes VAT
A diner pays a restaurant bill that includes sales tax
An investor pays tax on a gain from selling shares
A driver pays a price for petrol that includes fuel duty
sol: Tax on a gain is charged on the person who made the gain: direct.
VAT, sales tax and fuel duty are passed on in the price: indirect.

items.title: Tax base
items.rule:
The tax base is the thing being taxed. Three broad bases:

  • Income / profits: income tax, corporate income tax
  • Capital / wealth: capital gains tax, inheritance tax, wealth tax
  • Consumption: VAT, sales tax, excise duties
items.body: Different tiers of government lean on different bases. In the US: federal mostly income, states a mix of income and consumption, local mostly property.

items.title: Incidence: formal v effective
items.rule:
Formal incidence: who is legally required to pay the tax over to the authority.

Effective (actual) incidence: who ends up bearing the economic cost.
items.body:
TaxFormalEffective
VATRetailerCustomer
PAYEEmployerEmployee
items.trap: Exam questions say "from the shopper's point of view". Read whose viewpoint is asked before picking formal or effective.

items.q: A shopper pays ${price} for a coat, including sales tax. From the shopper's point of view, the sales tax is:
opts: a direct tax with formal incidence
an indirect tax with formal incidence
a direct tax with effective incidence
an indirect tax with effective incidence
sol: Sales tax is charged on spending and passed on: indirect.
The shopper doesn't pay it to the authority (the shop does) but bears the cost: effective incidence.
items.trap: Choosing formal because the shopper "pays" it. They pay the shop, not the tax authority.

alt.q: A shop sells a coat for $240 including sales tax and pays the tax it collects to the tax authority. From the shop's point of view, the sales tax is:
sol: Sales tax is indirect.
The shop is legally responsible for paying it over, so from its side the incidence is formal.
alt.trap: Choosing effective. The shop passes the cost on, so it does not bear it.

items.q: A bookshop adds sales tax to its prices and pays the tax it collects over to the tax authority. From the bookshop's point of view, the tax has:
opts: formal incidence
effective incidence
informal incidence
ineffective incidence
sol: The bookshop has the legal duty to pay the tax over: formal incidence.
The customer bears the cost: effective incidence. "Informal" and "ineffective" are not terms used.

alt.q: A bookshop adds sales tax to its prices and pays the tax it collects over to the tax authority. From the customer's point of view, the tax has:
sol: The customer bears the cost in the price: effective incidence.
The bookshop has the formal incidence.

items.title: Four terms the exam uses
items.rule:
TermMeaning
Taxable personThe individual or entity accountable for paying the tax.
Competent jurisdictionThe authority with legal power to assess and collect the tax (UK: HMRC). Its laws can be enforced against you.
HypothecationRing-fencing a tax's revenue for one purpose, e.g. London congestion charge → transport.
Tax gapTax that should in theory be collected minus tax actually collected.
items.trap: Competent jurisdiction is about whose laws can be enforced, not where the office is or where customers are.

items.q: "Hypothecation" means:
opts: tax law must be renewed each year for taxes to be collectable
the gap between tax due and tax actually collected
tax is withheld before income reaches the recipient
revenue from particular taxes is reserved for particular areas of spending
sol: Hypothecation = ring-fencing revenue from a tax for a specific purpose.
B is the tax gap; C is deduction at source (withholding).

opts: tax law must be renewed each year for taxes to be collectable
the gap between tax that should be collected and tax actually collected
tax is withheld before income reaches the recipient
revenue from particular taxes is reserved for particular areas of spending
sol: Tax gap = theoretical tax due − tax collected.
D describes hypothecation.

items.q: An entity is taxed in a "competent jurisdiction". This means the country:
opts: where its registered office building is located
whose tax laws can be enforced against the entity
where most of its customers are based
where most of its directors live
sol: A competent jurisdiction is the authority with legal power to assess and collect tax from the entity.
The test is enforceability of its laws, not the location of buildings, customers or people.

items.title: Progressive, proportional, regressive
items.rule:
Define the effective rate r(Y) = T / Y, tax as a fraction of income.

progressive: r rises as Y rises proportional: r constant regressive: r falls as Y rises
items.svg:

items.trap: Comparing dollar amounts. A regressive tax can still take more dollars from the richer person; only the % matters.
items.upd: UK 2026/27: income tax 20% / 40% / 45% (additional rate above £125,140). Employee NI 8% then 2% above £50,270, so NI has a regressive element. Exams give you the rates.

items.q: In Country P, Ash earns ${y1} and pays tax of ${t1}, and Birch earns ${y2} and pays ${t2}. The tax is:
opts: regressive
proportional
progressive
a flat-rate tax
sol: {?r1>r2|The higher earner pays a higher % → progressive.|The higher earner pays a lower % → regressive.}
items.trap: Ash pays more dollars whatever the structure. Compare % rates, not amounts.

items.q: In Country Q, Cedar earns ${y1} and pays tax of ${t1}, and Dale earns ${y2} and pays ${t2}. The tax is:
opts: regressive
proportional
progressive
a lump-sum tax
sol: {?abs(r1-r2)<1e-9|Same % at both incomes → proportional.|{?r1>r2|Higher earner, higher % → progressive.|Higher earner, lower % → regressive.}}
items.trap: Seeing a bigger dollar bill for the richer person and calling it progressive.

items.q: In the same country, Fenn earns taxable profit of ${y1} and pays tax of ${t1}. Garr earns ${y2} and pays ${t2}. The tax is best described as:
opts: progressive
regressive
proportional
indirect
sol: {?t2/y2>t1/y1|The effective rate rises with profit → progressive.|The effective rate falls as profit rises → regressive.}
items.trap: Tax on profit is direct, so "indirect" is never the answer here.

items.title: Sources of tax rules
items.rule:
• Legislation: e.g. the annual UK Finance Acts
  • Precedent and authority guidance: case law plus the authority's published practice (HMRC statements of practice)
  • Directives from international bodies: e.g. EU VAT directives
  • Agreements between countries: double tax treaties
items.trap: "International law" in general, or a foreign court's judgment, is not a source of a country's own tax rules. Specific treaties and directives are.
items.upd: Since 2024 many countries apply the OECD "Pillar Two" 15% global minimum tax for groups with revenue of €750m+. Chapter 3 has the detail.

items.q: Which of the following would NOT normally be a source of a country's own tax rules?
opts: Tax statutes passed by the national parliament
Tax treaties the country has signed with other states
Published practice notes issued by the national tax authority
Judgments of the courts of a foreign country
sol: Domestic legislation, treaties and the authority's published practice are all sources.
A foreign court's judgment is not binding on another country.

alt.q: Which of the following IS normally a source of a country's own tax rules?
opts: Judgments of the courts of a foreign country
International law in general
A double tax treaty the country has signed
Opinions published by tax advisers
sol: Treaties the country has signed are a source of its tax rules.
Foreign judgments, "international law" in general and adviser opinions are not.

items.title: Unit v ad valorem; excise duty
items.rule:
TypeBased onExample
Unit taxQuantity: number, weight, volume. Price doesn't matter.Excise duty: $X per litre
Ad valoremValue: a % of the priceSales tax, VAT
items.body:
Excise duties sit on alcohol, tobacco, fuel and vehicles: to discourage harmful consumption, cover the public costs it causes, and tax luxuries.

Best-suited goods: few large producers (easy to collect), inelastic demand with no close substitutes, high volumes, easy to define.
items.trap: Excise works on goods people keep buying when the price rises. Putting it on price-sensitive (elastic) goods would kill the revenue.

items.q: A government charges ${rate#2} on every kilogram of sugar used in soft drinks, whatever the drink's selling price. This is:
opts: an ad valorem tax
a unit tax
a direct tax
a value added tax
sol: The tax depends on quantity (kilograms), not price → unit tax.
It is an excise-type duty: indirect, not direct.

alt.q: A government charges 12% of the selling price on every soft drink sold, whatever its sugar content. This is:
sol: A % of value → ad valorem.
It is a single sales charge, not a multi-stage VAT, and it is indirect.

items.q: Which is NOT a reason for putting a specific excise duty on a category of goods?
opts: To raise revenue from luxuries that people buy whatever the price
To discourage consumption of harmful goods such as cigarettes
To help fund the health costs that harmful goods cause
To raise revenue from goods whose demand is very price-sensitive
sol: Excise suits goods with inelastic demand: buyers keep buying, so revenue holds up.
Price-sensitive (elastic) demand would collapse when the duty is added, so D is not a reason.
items.trap: Reading "raise revenue" in D and ticking it as a valid reason. The elastic part is what makes it wrong.

alt.q: Which of the following goods is BEST suited to a specific excise duty?
opts: A product with many small producers and close substitutes
A product with inelastic demand made by a few large producers
A product whose demand is very price-sensitive
A product that is hard to define or measure
sol: Ideal excise goods: inelastic demand, few large producers, high volumes, easy to define.
Each other option undermines collection or revenue.

items.title: Property, wealth and consumption taxes
items.rule:
• Property taxes: on capital or rental value, e.g. UK Stamp Duty Land Tax.
  • Wealth taxes: on total wealth (pensions, artworks…). Few countries use them.
  • Single-stage consumption tax: charged at one level only (manufacturing, wholesale or retail). US sales tax is retail-level.
  • Multi-stage: charged every time the product changes hands. Two forms: cascade (no refunds, so tax compounds and becomes a cost) and VAT (businesses reclaim input tax).
items.trap: Cascade tax won't be calculated in the exam, but you must know it differs from VAT: no reclaim, so it compounds.

items.q: Which is a feature of a multi-stage sales tax?
opts: The rate rises as profits rise
Tax is charged at every stage of the production and distribution chain
Tax is charged only at the final retail sale
Tax applies only to luxury items
sol: Multi-stage = charged each time the product is sold along the chain (cascade or VAT).
C describes a single-stage retail tax.

alt.q: Which is a feature of a single-stage sales tax?
opts: The rate rises as profits rise
Tax is charged at every stage of the production and distribution chain
Tax is charged at only one level of the chain, such as the final retail sale
Businesses reclaim the tax they pay on purchases
sol: Single-stage = one level of the chain only, e.g. US retail sales tax.
B describes multi-stage; D describes VAT.

items.title: VAT: output minus input
items.rule:
VAT payable = output tax − input tax

Output tax: VAT charged on sales. Input tax: VAT paid on purchases.

Sum over the chain: each business pays r × (its value added), so total VAT = r × final consumer price. The whole burden lands on the consumer.

items.q: VAT is charged at {r%}. A grower sells wheat to a miller for ${s1} (net of VAT). The miller sells flour to a baker for ${s2} (net). The baker sells bread to consumers for ${s3} (net). How much VAT does the miller pay to the tax authority?
sol: Miller output tax = {s2} × {r%} = {=s2*r}
Miller input tax = {s1} × {r%} = {=s1*r}
Payable = {=s2*r} − {=s1*r} = {=s2*r-s1*r}
items.trap: Paying VAT on the whole sale price ({=s2*r}) and forgetting to deduct the input tax already paid to the grower.

items.title: Zero-rated v exempt
items.rule:
SupplyVAT on saleReclaim input VAT?
Standard / higher ratedStandard or higher rateYes
Zero rated0%Yes
ExemptNone: outside VATNo
items.body:
Zero-rated is still a taxable supply at 0%, so input VAT is reclaimable. Exempt is outside the system, so input VAT becomes a real cost.

UK examples: zero-rated = basic food, children's clothes, exports. Exempt = finance, insurance. The exam tells you the category.
items.trap: Both charge no VAT on the sale, so they look identical. The difference is entirely on the input side.

items.q: Which statement about a business making only zero-rated supplies is correct?
opts: It charges no VAT and cannot reclaim input VAT
It charges no VAT but can reclaim input VAT on its purchases
It charges VAT at the standard rate and reclaims input VAT
It is outside the VAT system and need not register
sol: Zero-rated supplies are taxable at 0%.
Because they are taxable, input VAT is recoverable, and the business often gets repayments.
items.trap: Treating zero-rated like exempt. A is the exempt position.

alt.q: Which statement about a business making only exempt supplies is correct?
opts: It charges no VAT and cannot reclaim input VAT
It charges no VAT but can reclaim input VAT on its purchases
It charges VAT at 0% and gets repayments
It must register for VAT and file quarterly returns
sol: Exempt supplies are outside VAT: no output tax.
Input VAT on purchases can't be reclaimed, so it becomes part of the business's costs.
alt.trap: Answering B, which is the zero-rated position.

items.q: For the quarter, sales excluding tax are: standard-rated ${std}, zero-rated ${zero}, exempt ${ex}. Purchases including tax are: for standard-rated sales ${pstd}; for zero-rated sales ${pzero}; for exempt sales ${pex}. Sales tax is {r%}. How much sales tax is due for the quarter? Give your answer to the nearest $.
sol: Output tax: only standard-rated sales carry tax. {std} × {r%} = {=std*r}
Input tax on standard-rated purchases: {pstd} × {r%}/(1 + {r%}) = {=pstd*r/(1+r)}
Input tax on zero-rated purchases: {pzero} × 20/120 = {=pzero*r/(1+r)}. Zero-rated is taxable, so this is reclaimable.
Exempt-related purchases: no reclaim.
Due = {=std*r} − {=pstd*r/(1+r)} − {=pzero*r/(1+r)} = {=rd(std*r - pstd*r/(1+r) - pzero*r/(1+r))}
items.trap: Two traps: taking 20% of the tax-inclusive purchase figures (use 20/120), and reclaiming input tax on exempt-related purchases.

items.title: VAT from a gross price
items.rule: net price given: VAT = net × r gross price given: VAT = gross × r/(1 + r) at 20%: gross × 20/120 = gross ÷ 6
items.body: Dimensional check: gross = net × (1 + r), so net = gross/(1 + r) and VAT = gross − net = gross × r/(1 + r).
items.trap: 124 × 20% = 24.80 is wrong: that taxes the tax. (Your book's margin note shows 20.66; it should round to 20.67.)

items.q: A customer pays ${g} for a jacket, including VAT at {r%}. How much of the price is VAT? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
sol: The price is gross, so VAT = gross × r/(1 + r).
items.trap: Taking {r%} of the gross price ({=g*r#2}) taxes the VAT itself.

items.q: In a quarter a trader's taxable outputs are ${out} and taxable inputs are ${inp}, both net of sales tax at {r%}. The position with the tax authority is:
opts: ${=abs(out-inp)*r} recoverable
${=abs(out-inp)*r} payable
${=abs(out-inp)*r/(1+r)#2} payable
${=abs(out-inp)*r/(1+r)#2} recoverable
sol: Figures are net, so multiply by {r%} directly.
Output tax {=out*r}; input tax {=inp*r}.
{?out>inp|Output exceeds input: {=(out-inp)*r} payable.|Input exceeds output: {=(inp-out)*r} recoverable (a repayment).}
items.trap: Using r/(1 + r) on net figures. That fraction is only for tax-inclusive amounts.

items.title: VAT registration and administration
items.rule:
A taxable person making taxable supplies (standard, higher or zero-rated) must register once taxable turnover passes the threshold.

Once registered: issue VAT invoices, keep records, charge VAT, reclaim input VAT on purchases used for taxable supplies, file returns (UK: quarterly) and pay.
items.body: Blocked input VAT (UK): cars (unless bought for resale, e.g. by a dealer) and business entertaining (unless for staff).
items.upd: UK registration threshold £90,000 since 1 April 2024 (deregistration £88,000). Rates 20% / 5% / 0%.

items.q: Under the UK-style rules in your study text, input VAT on which TWO of the following purchases by a VAT-registered manufacturer is blocked (not recoverable)?
opts: A company car for the sales director
Raw materials used in production
A dinner to entertain key customers
A staff summer party
sol: Cars are blocked unless bought for resale. A manufacturer isn't a car dealer.
Customer entertaining is blocked; staff entertaining is not.
Raw materials for taxable supplies: fully recoverable.

items.title: Employee tax and PAYE
items.rule:
Employees are taxed on earnings: salary, bonus, commission and benefits in kind (company car, accommodation, cheap loans, medical insurance), less allowable expenses and allowances.

Why collect at source (PAYE)?

  • Less risk of default: tax is taken before the employee gets paid
  • Regular receipts help the government budget its cash flow
  • The authority deals with one employer, not many employees
  • The employer bears most of the admin cost
items.body: Basis of assessment varies: France taxes last year's earnings, Switzerland the average of two years, the UK the current year's receipts. You won't compute employee tax in F1.
items.trap: PAYE does not reduce the employee's total tax. It changes when and how it is collected, not how much.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of collecting employee income tax through PAYE?
opts: Employees pay in small amounts through the year rather than one large bill
Government can predict its tax receipts more easily
It reduces the total amount of tax the employee has to pay
Government receives the cash sooner
sol: PAYE changes timing and collection, not the liability.
A, B and D are genuine benefits.

alt.q: Which of the following IS a benefit to government of collecting employee income tax through PAYE?
opts: It reduces the total amount of tax the employee has to pay
It removes the need for any tax records
Tax is collected before the employee receives the pay, reducing default
Employees choose when they pay
sol: Deduction at source cuts default risk and gives regular receipts.
PAYE doesn't change the liability or remove record-keeping.

items.q: Statements about PAYE: (i) employers carry most of the administration cost; (ii) some employers hold on to deducted tax or never pay it over; (iii) employers may make mistakes in what they deduct; (iv) fewer late payments and defaults mean government collects more of the tax due. Which two would government NOT see as advantages?
opts: (i) and (ii)
(ii) and (iii)
(ii) and (iv)
(iii) and (iv)
sol: (i) is an advantage to government: someone else carries the admin cost.
(iv) is an advantage: less default.
(ii) withheld-but-unpaid tax and (iii) deduction errors are drawbacks.
items.trap: Ticking (i) as a disadvantage. It's bad for employers, but the question asks from government's viewpoint.

alt.q: Statements about PAYE: (i) employers carry most of the administration cost; (ii) some employers hold on to deducted tax or never pay it over; (iii) employers may make mistakes in what they deduct; (iv) fewer late payments and defaults mean government collects more of the tax due. Which two WOULD government see as advantages?
opts: (i) and (ii)
(ii) and (iii)
(i) and (iv)
(iii) and (iv)
sol: (i): the admin cost sits with employers, not government.
(iv): fewer defaults.
(ii) and (iii) are drawbacks.

items.q: Which is NOT an advantage to the tax authority of deducting tax at source?
opts: It is easier to work out each taxpayer's total liability for the period
The tax arrives sooner
The paying organisation bears the administration cost
Tax is taken before the recipient receives the money
sol: Deduction at source collects tax early and shifts admin to the payer.
It does not make the total liability easier to compute: the taxpayer may have other income, so a year-end calculation is still needed.
items.trap: A sounds plausible because tax is "already sorted". Withholding is collection, not assessment.

alt.q: Which IS an advantage to the tax authority of deducting tax at source?
opts: It makes each taxpayer's total liability easier to compute
The tax arrives sooner and default is less likely
The tax authority bears the administration cost
The recipient can choose when to pay
sol: Deduction at source brings cash in early and cuts default.
The payer, not the authority, carries the admin cost; total liability still needs working out.

items.title: Administration: records, deadlines, powers
items.rule:
Records: corporate tax (accounts + tax workings), VAT (invoices, day books, VAT account), overseas subsidiaries (transfer-pricing documentation), employee tax (deductions, year-end returns, employee statements). UK retention: 6 years.

Assessment: either the authority assesses, or the taxpayer self-assesses (UK, USA) and the authority checks.

Powers: query returns, demand special reports, examine earlier years' records (US: up to 20 years), enter premises and seize documents, share information with foreign authorities.
items.body: Why set deadlines? Taxpayers know when to pay; the authority can forecast receipts; there's a clear trigger for penalties; employers can't use PAYE deductions as free working capital.
items.trap: Power of arrest or detention is the power a tax authority is least likely to have. That belongs to the police.

items.q: Which power is a tax authority LEAST likely to have?
opts: Power to detain a taxpayer in custody
Power to inspect a business's accounting records
Power to enter premises and search for documents
Power to exchange information with overseas tax authorities
sol: Inspection, search and information-sharing are standard tax-authority powers.
Detention is a police or court power.

alt.q: Which power is a tax authority MOST likely to have?
opts: Power to detain a taxpayer in custody
Power to sentence a taxpayer to prison
Power to examine records from previous years
Power to arrest a company director
sol: Examining earlier years' records is a standard power (US: up to 20 years back).
Detention, arrest and sentencing are police or court powers.

items.q: Which THREE of the following are reasons why a tax system benefits from fixed due dates for filing returns and paying tax?
opts: Taxpayers know exactly when payment is due
The authority can forecast its cash receipts
Deadlines reduce the amount of tax payable
They give a clear trigger for late-payment penalties and interest
They let employers keep PAYE deductions as working capital for longer
sol: A, B and D are the standard reasons.
Deadlines don't change the liability (C).
E is the opposite: deadlines stop employers using deducted tax as free finance.

items.q: Under a self-assessment system:
opts: the tax authority calculates each taxpayer's liability and issues a bill
the taxpayer calculates and reports their own liability, and the authority checks it
no returns are filed because tax is deducted at source
tax is only payable once the authority has audited the return
sol: Self-assessment (UK, USA): the taxpayer works out and declares the liability.
The authority then reviews and can query or investigate.

items.title: Tax avoidance v tax evasion
items.rule:
What it isMain risk
AvoidanceLegal: arranging affairs within the law to pay lessReputational ("not paying a fair share")
EvasionIllegal: deliberately breaking the lawProsecution, fines, penalties
items.body: How authorities fight both: deduct at source and use third-party reporting; simplify (fewer reliefs to exploit); audit more; communicate well; build a system seen as fair; review penalties.
items.trap: Avoidance being legal doesn't make it risk-free. Exam answers on its risk point to reputation, not prosecution.

items.q: Classify each action as tax avoidance or tax evasion.
items: Locating a subsidiary in a low-tax country to cut the group's tax bill
Timing a capital purchase to claim a 100% first-year allowance
sol: Evasion = deliberately breaking the law: under-declaring income, fictitious expenses.
Avoidance = legal arrangements: low-tax subsidiary, timing purchases to use allowances the law offers.
items.trap: Calling the low-tax subsidiary "evasion" because it feels wrong. It's legal (avoidance); the risk is reputational.

items.q: A large retailer is criticised in the press for routing profits through a low-tax country, entirely within the law. The MAIN risk it faces is:
opts: criminal prosecution for tax evasion
reputational damage and loss of customers
automatic penalties from its home tax authority
loss of its competent jurisdiction
sol: The arrangement is legal, so it is avoidance, not evasion: no prosecution.
The risk is reputational: being seen as not paying a fair share.

items.q: Which of the following measures mainly reduces the OPPORTUNITY for tax evasion?
opts: Deducting tax at source and third-party reporting
Running advertising about the fairness of the system
Increasing the number of reliefs and allowances
Raising tax rates
sol: If tax is taken before income reaches the taxpayer, or a third party reports the income, there is little left to hide.
More reliefs (C) increase complexity and exploitation; B works on attitudes, not opportunity.

alt.q: Which measure mainly works by changing SOCIAL ATTITUDES to paying tax?
opts: Deducting tax at source
Third-party reporting of income
Making the system honest, simple and seen as fair
Auditing more returns
sol: A system seen as fair builds commitment to paying.
A and B reduce opportunity; D increases detection.

items.title: Direct tax on trading income: the identity
items.rule:
Taxable profit = Accounting profit − exempt / other-rules income + disallowable expenses + accounting depreciation − tax depreciation

Then tax = taxable profit × rate. The question always gives the country's rules.
items.trap: Depreciation is swapped, not netted against anything else: add back the book figure, deduct the tax authority's figure.

items.q: Delta Co reports profit before tax of ${pbt}. This includes ${ex} of dividend income, which is exempt, and ${ent} of client entertaining, which is disallowable. Accounting depreciation is ${dep} and tax depreciation is ${tdep}. The tax rate is {r%}. Calculate the tax payable.
sol: Taxable profit = {pbt} − {ex} + {ent} + {dep} − {tdep} = {=pbt-ex+ent+dep-tdep}
Tax = {=pbt-ex+ent+dep-tdep} × {r%} = {=(pbt-ex+ent+dep-tdep)*r}
items.trap: Adding the exempt income back instead of deducting it. It is already in PBT, so it has to come out.

items.title: Capital taxes: the gain identity
items.rule: Gain = (proceeds − selling costs) − cost − buying costs − enhancement − indexation (if allowed)
items.body: Capital taxes hit gains on disposing of investments and non-current assets. Most countries use historical cost; a few index costs for inflation. Chapter 2 drills this.
items.upd: UK company indexation was frozen at December 2017 and individuals' was abolished in 2008. Exam questions set in a hypothetical country can still give an indexation factor.

items.q: A company sells a warehouse for ${pr} and pays ${sc} in agents' fees. It bought the warehouse for ${cost} with ${bc} of legal costs, and later spent ${enh} on an extension. The indexation factor on all allowable costs is {ix%}. Calculate the chargeable gain.
sol: Net proceeds = {pr} − {sc} = {=pr-sc}
Allowable costs = {cost} + {bc} + {enh} = {=cost+bc+enh}
Indexation = {ix%} × {=cost+bc+enh} = {=(cost+bc+enh)*ix}
Gain = {=pr-sc} − {=cost+bc+enh} − {=(cost+bc+enh)*ix} = {=pr-sc-(cost+bc+enh)*(1+ix)}
items.trap: Indexing only the purchase price. Here the factor applies to every allowable cost, including legal fees and the extension.
